summary: Defines terms used when benchmarking ATM based switching devices, so test results can be described and compared consistently. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM switches are measured against each other, but only if everyone uses the same words for what they measured. RFC 2761 is the vocabulary for benchmarking ATM equipment: what a cell is, what the traffic parameters mean, and what each performance metric counts.

questions: what is constant bit rate cbr service
what is cell loss priority clp
how does aal5 affect tcp throughput
subtitle: The shared vocabulary for measuring ATM switches and the links between them

tldr.problem: Performance figures for ATM equipment are only comparable if everyone uses the same words for what they measured, and the ATM literature had no single agreed set of those words.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines 58 formal terms for ATM and its traffic parameters, and then 20 performance metrics with their units, grouped by the layers of the B-ISDN model so that a physical layer count is never confused with an ATM layer count.
tldr.outcome: The result is a reference vocabulary, not a protocol. It records how each ATM parameter affects IP and TCP throughput, which is the reason the terms matter beyond the test lab.

facts.label: ATM cell size
facts.value: 53 octets: a 5-octet header and a 48-octet payload

facts.label: Cell header fields
facts.value: GFC 4 bits, VPI 8, VCI 16, PT 3, CLP 1, HEC 8

facts.value: 20, grouped by layer: 3 physical, 7 ATM, 3 AAL5, 5 signalling, 2 ILMI

today: RFC 2761 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a terminology document, not a protocol, and the working group that wrote it also publishes separate methodology documents describing how to collect each benchmark it names.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The memo defines terms for performance benchmarking tests and their results in the context of ATM switching devices. It extends terminology already defined for benchmarking network interconnect devices in RFC 1242, RFC 2285 and RFC 2544, and its focus is on ATM cell relay and signalling, although some of the definitions could apply to a broader group of devices.

It has two major parts. The first is Background, which explains the reference model and the assumptions behind the document. The second is Definitions, split into formal definitions, provided as a courtesy to the reader and subsumed from other work inside and outside the IETF, and measurement definitions, which give performance metrics with inherent units. The divisions of the measurement part follow the B-ISDN model.

The document assumes the necessary services are available and active: IP connectivity requires SSCOP connectivity between signalling entities, and the system under test is assumed to be able to configure ATM addresses, whether hard coded or through ILMI or PNNI neighbour discovery, to run SSCOP, and to perform signalled call setups through UNI or PNNI signalling. It covers only the CBR, VBR and UBR traffic types, leaving ABR to a separate document, and it presents only the terminology associated with benchmarking IP performance over ATM, so it is not a complete compilation of ATM test terminology. The working group that produced it also produces methodology documents, which define the procedures for collecting the benchmarks cited in the terminology documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Two switches can be measured, but the numbers only mean the same thing if both tests were described in the same words. This memo supplies those words for ATM equipment: what a cell is, what the traffic parameters mean, and what each measurement counts.

sections.title: The B-ISDN Model and the ATM Cell
sections.content:
The B-ISDN model has four layers and two planes. The service layer carries IP in the user plane, with ILMI, UNI and PNNI in the control plane. Below it the adaptation layer carries AAL1, AAL2, AAL3/4 and AAL5 in the user plane and SAAL in the control plane. Below that the ATM layer does cell relay in the user plane and OAM and resource management in the control plane, and at the bottom the physical layer covers convergence and media.

ATM itself organises information into cells of 53 octets. It is asynchronous in the sense that the recurrence of cells from an individual user is not necessarily periodic, and unlike ISDN it uses fixed length cells, which is why higher layer PDUs have to be adapted into ATM by one of the four adaptation layers. A cell is a 5-octet header followed by a 48-octet payload. The header carries generic flow control in 4 bits, the virtual path identifier in 8 bits, the virtual channel identifier in 16 bits, the payload type in 3 bits, the cell loss priority in 1 bit, and a header error check of 8 bits, a CRC computed over the previous four octets. The generic flow control field has local significance only, and the value encoded in it is not carried end to end.

The adaptation layers are AAL1 for circuit emulation, AAL2 for sub-rated voice over ATM, AAL3/4 for data over noisy ATM lines, and AAL5 for data over ATM, the most widely used type. AAL5 adapts multi-cell higher layer PDUs into ATM with minimal error checking and no error detection. Its CPCS PDU holds the higher layer PDU, padding if needed so that the trailer occupies the final eight octets of the last cell, and then the trailer itself: a one-octet user-to-user indication, a one-octet common part indicator that must be set to 0, a two-octet length of the higher layer PDU, and a 32-bit CRC over the entire PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM traffic travels in fixed packets of 53 bytes: a 5-byte header and 48 bytes of content. The header says which virtual channel the packet belongs to and whether it may be dropped first when the network is busy. Above that layer, one of four adaptation types packs ordinary network data into the cells, and AAL5, the common one, adds a small trailer with a checksum.

sections.title: Traffic Descriptors and Contracts
sections.content:
An ATM traffic descriptor is a generic list of traffic parameters specifying the intrinsic traffic characteristics of a requested connection. It must include the peak cell rate and the quality of service class, and may include burst tolerance, the sustainable cell rate and a best effort indicator. The traffic contract is the agreement between the user and the network about those parameters.

Conformance with the contract is defined by the Generic Cell Rate Algorithm, which for each arriving cell decides whether that cell conforms. It has two parameters, the increment and the limit. For CBR the increment is 1/PCR and the limit is the cell delay variation tolerance. For VBR there are two such algorithms running, a dual leaky bucket: the first behaves as for CBR, and the second polices cells that already conform to the first, using an increment of 1/SCR and a limit of burst tolerance.

The individual parameters then have their own meanings. The peak cell rate is the maximum rate at which the user may send cells. The sustainable cell rate is an upper bound on the conforming average rate of the connection over time scales long relative to those of the peak cell rate, so the network can allocate fewer resources than the peak would need and still meet its performance objectives. Burst tolerance, together with the sustainable cell rate, specifies the maximum number of cells that will be accepted at the peak cell rate, and it is the limit parameter of the second algorithm. The maximum burst size is expressed in cells. Connection admission control is the set of actions the network takes during call setup, or re-negotiation, to decide whether a connection request can be accepted or should be rejected, based on the traffic descriptor and on the presented and existing load, and possibly on administrative policies such as the calling party number required or access limitations. Usage parameter control is the enforcement side of the same contract.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ATM connection comes with a list of rules: how fast it may send, how much it may burst, and what the network promises in return. The network checks those rules cell by cell with a formula called the generic cell rate algorithm, and it may refuse a connection that would not fit the capacity available.

sections.title: Segmentation, Reassembly and Loss
sections.content:
Segmentation and reassembly is the process the adaptation layer uses to fragment higher layer PDUs into ATM cells. It is not itself a measurement, but the speed at which it is performed can be, and the way it is performed greatly affects performance. It can be done on the interface card, on board, or in machine central memory, in core. On-board computation should give only a small, constant delay, while in-core computation gives a variable delay, which will negatively affect TCP round trip time computations. The location of the CRC-32 calculation complicates this further: with an in-core CRC-32, bus contention may make on-board segmentation slower than in-core segmentation. On-board CRC-32 calculation and segmentation together give the most favourable performance results.

ATM layer impairments also affect segmentation and reassembly. Cell error, cell loss, cell mis-insertion and cell delay variation all have a negative effect. A cell error makes an AAL5 PDU fail its CRC-32 check and be discarded, so the packet it carried is lost. Cell loss and mis-insertion make a PDU fail its length check and be discarded, and the outcome depends on which cell was lost. If a cell with payload type indicator 0 is lost, re-assembly registers a length discrepancy and discards the PDU. If the cell with payload type indicator 1 is lost, several things can happen: the re-assembly timer may expire before the first cell of the next PDU arrives, in which case the incomplete PDU is discarded and one packet is lost; the first cell of the next PDU may arrive first, in which case the incomplete PDU is prepended to the next one, and then either the timer expires and both are discarded, losing two packets, or the last cell arrives in time and a length discrepancy is registered and both are discarded, again losing two packets; or a mechanism that identifies the start of a higher layer PDU, such as IP, discards the cells of the first incomplete PDU, losing one packet.

Other impairments have their own effect on TCP. Large cell delay variation values will adversely affect TCP throughput and cause a segmentation and re-assembly timeout. Cells presented to an interface that violate burst tolerance may be dropped, which causes AAL5 PDU corruption, and burst tolerance also affects the TCP round trip time calculation. The cell loss priority bit gives two levels of priority, with cells marked 0 higher priority than cells marked 1, and cells marked 1 may be discarded during congestion to preserve the cell loss ratio of the cells marked 0. An explicit forward congestion indication in the payload type field lets a network element that is congested or nearly so alert the destination, which may then lower the rate of the connection; in the case of TCP, the receiver could acknowledge the current segment and set the window size to a very small number.
sections.plainLanguage: Two pieces of data put together at the far end of an ATM link can be torn apart by a single lost cell. The memo lists what happens in each case: sometimes one packet is lost, sometimes two, and sometimes the receiver has to wait for a timer before it knows something is wrong. It also says where the work of packing and unpacking is done has a real effect, because doing it in software adds a variable delay that TCP notices.

sections.title: The Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The measurement part defines each metric in the same shape used for the formal definitions, with the metric itself, its definition, a discussion of its application and any restrictions on measurement procedures, and the intrinsic units used to quantify it, where subsidiary units such as microseconds are acceptable if the intrinsic unit is seconds. The metrics are grouped by the layers of the B-ISDN model.

At the physical layer, which the memo takes to be SONET, three metrics are defined: pointer movements, the number of changes in a SONET pointer due to clock synchronisation slips, measured per second; the transport overhead error count, the number of transport overhead errors detected, which cause SONET frames carrying IP datagrams to be lost; and the path overhead error count, which counts path overhead errors with the same effect.

At the ATM layer there are seven. Cell delay variation is the variation in cell transfer delay associated with a given traffic load, orientation and distribution, and with an integration period. Cell transfer delay is the elapsed time between a cell exit event at one measurement point and the corresponding cell entry event at another for a particular connection, which is the sum of the total inter-node transmission delay and the total node processing delay; the memo notes that while this number should be constant it is a component in the round trip time. Cell error ratio, cell loss ratio and cell misinsertion ratio count damaged, lost and wrongly inserted cells against the cells successfully transmitted. The cell rate margin measures the difference between the effective bandwidth allocation and the allocation for sustainable rate in cells per second, which shows how much provisioned bandwidth goes unused because of encapsulation overhead or because TCP usually transmits in only one direction. The CRC error ratio is the ratio of received PDUs with an invalid CRC to the total number of cells properly transmitted, and it can be measured in service with a test probe at the transmission convergence layer.

Three metrics belong to AAL5: re-assembly errors, re-assembly time and a CRC error ratio. Five belong to signalling: the time for connection admission control to decide that a call must be rejected, which is under four seconds where Call Proceeding is implemented and under ten seconds otherwise; connection establishment time, from the first Setup message to the Connect message; connection teardown time, from the Release message to the Release Complete; crankback time, when a blocked designated transit list forces the call to be re-routed; and route update response time. Two belong to ILMI: MIB alignment time and address registration time.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurements are sorted by layer, so a physical layer count of lost frames is never confused with an ATM layer count of lost cells. Each one says what it counts and in what unit, from seconds for call setup time to cells per second for unused bandwidth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it is solely for providing terminology and describes neither a protocol nor an implementation, so it has no security considerations of its own. It notes that a number of the definitions discuss how a particular ATM parameter affects IP or TCP, and that the effect of administrative policies on performance is outside its scope and handled by the benchmarking terminology document for firewall performance.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing to secure here, because the memo defines words rather than a protocol or a product. The only security-relevant thing it does is point out which parameters affect TCP behaviour.

fields.name: GFC
fields.desc: Generic flow control. Local significance only; the value is not carried end to end.

fields.name: CLP
fields.desc: Cell loss priority. Cells marked 1 may be discarded during congestion.

fields.desc: Header error check, a CRC computed over the previous four octets.
